That's where we started, right? Well, you know.

blocks.s: Mrs. George Henderson (wife of George Henderson)
blocks.x: When I come back home, I was born around 19-something.

I was working at that oil station and Sam Peck come down and got me and said, I want to put music on Ja'Kaula Street. You want to come and work? I said, yeah, I'd better be waiting around that and be waiting at the oil station. I don't know if that's when I went there. I don't know if that's when I went there. And you was playing at that other place. Yeah. Well, when was that you all went to New York on the boat? When year was it? 1930. 1930. 1930, I remember. Yeah, 1930. Did that trip take long? I forget. 17-day round trip. It was on a steam at Dixie. Yeah. Did you make several trips? Well, I made one trip in 1930.

blocks.s: Mrs. George Henderson (wife of George Henderson)
blocks.x: They got seasick. They kind of disgust them. They all got their belly.

They had one bamboo What other bands you played with besides the Camellia? Black Diamond? Yeah. Well now I substitute in a lot of bands. Like what? Like Buddy Petit. I played with substitute with his. You played on Buddy Petit? I played with Buddy. I played with Kid Howard. I played with Omar. Omar was a nice trumpet in these days, but I don't believe in the ... but he was on record in the way of speaking. You remember Omar? Yeah. I played with him a lot. Well when you played with these different bands, George, did you have to play differently for different bands, or did they ask you to play any special way? No. In fact most of the musicians knew what was going to be played in a way of speaking. They wouldn't come up with nothing that you didn't know. And you just keep your study time for all those bands? Well before we had a tempo headed to the same ocean. In fact the different drummer had different tempo. Some can raise it up and some can bring it down. That's the way the musicians had thought. Because playing would depend on a drummer. In those days because you could either raise the time or increase the time or lessen the time. You had to be just so in a way of speaking to the band. Well if you were considered a good musician, I mean a good drummer at that time, you could almost, after you played the first couple of numbers with the band playing, you could almost judge what you had to do. You could almost judge what you had to do. You could do something. You could almost judge what you had to do. You're figuring the band out. And you see in the brass section, well some bands were powerful than others. And that's how you could tell. Well some were weaker than others. And the style of playing was going to be different. Well the drummer would know just about what was going to happen, what to do. Because he could liven up a band at that time and then he could bring a band down. Just playing. Well I didn't know music, we're not orchestration. With orchestration you have to play what you see and do just what you're supposed to do. But at that time you played what you call that live. Just play according to your feelings. And did you find that you could, as you say, you could uplift the band? Well some, some. Well that's certain, certainly. Some band you certainly could. Because the drummer can feel it. They can feel it when you're doing wrong. You can feel it when they're not playing right like you would like to. Because there's a lot of passages you would like to make, or you can't make it on account of the way they're playing. You know, with brass, you want to make a break or something. Well you couldn't do it the way the brass instrument was carrying lead in a way of speaking. So is there any way that you can correct this? Yeah, yeah. There's a certain way that drummers had it could hit a lick and that bass drum would dead and everything almost. A certain way that you could hit and make everybody stop and look around. Bring them along. You know, they didn't use much mute on bass drums in them days, you know. No. They didn't use much mute. They used not to mute the drum now. Yeah, they put a little pad on it now. Oh yeah, they muted it down. Before the bass, I mean they had a small cymbal on the side, down at your foot pedal, and a little gadget. When you did, well it all would hit up against this little cymbal and sound together. Well, after they stopped using that, they took that little piece off and stopped using that little cymbal line. But they had a cymbal onto the drum, down on the bottom, and on your beater, on your beater, they had a little, the cymbal was here, and on the beater they had a little gadget that would hit it. When you'd hit, it would hit this, it would sound this cymbal line here too. Well, they eventually done a rave, they'd done away with that cymbal. That was a cymbal that worked just the same as the modern cymbals, sort of, well down, or did it come from over the top? No, it wasn't from the top. After they got rid of that overhead, that's what they used. It was a small cymbal attached to the drum. See, on the side of the bass drum like this, there was a beater, when the beater hit the drum, this gadget hit the cymbal like that, you see? A little separate arm coming up the beater. Yeah, a little cymbal, so big, you know. But it was sound. Yeah. I guess he's gone, Gifford, he might have it. Yeah, he's gone. Who else was in that band when you all went to New York? Oh, it was Mike, at the first time, Mike DeLay on trumpet, Casimir Paul played guitar, Bernard Santiago Abel played piano, Cleo played bass, and George Ellison played drum. He was very good bass, yeah. Very good. He could pick a bass man. This is not one of them, but there was something on his order. Oh, yeah. You see? Yeah, and it was hooked on, you'd hook that onto your bass drum. Oh, onto the rim of the bass drum. The rim of the bass drum, yeah. Now your foot pedal was here, and it had a little gadget. When you hit your bass drum, you'd hit this too. Inside of the cymbal. Oh, I see, yeah. So if you were beating, supposing you were beating four, four times, you would hit the bass drum four times? No, that way you wouldn't use this gadget, you see? Ah. Good, man. You wouldn't use the cymbal. You wouldn't use the cymbal. Well, what would you use the cymbal for? Slow foxtrot. Oh, on the cymbal. Oh, on to the rim of the bass drum. Oh, on to the rim of the bass drum. Yeah. Now your foot pedal was here, and it had a little gadget. When you hit your bass drum, you'd hit this too. It hit the inside of the cymbal. Inside of the cymbal. Inside of the cymbal. Oh, I see. Yeah. So if you were beating, supposing you were beating four, four times, you would hit the bass drum four times? No, that way you wouldn't use this gadget, you see? Ah. Good, man. You wouldn't use the cymbal. You wouldn't use the cymbal. Use this. Well, what would you use the cymbal for? Slow foxtrot. Uh-huh. And the walls too, if you hit it. In other words, like when you were hitting, let's say, two beats or one beat? Yeah, one or two. One, yeah. One or two. Yeah. I never used it on a four-four, no. No, no. Yeah, and it's just about that size. Just about that size, yeah. That's about what? About a nine inch or eight inch? That's about nine inches. That's about nine. About nine. Uh-huh. I never did see that attachment before. That goes right on the rim of the drum. Right on the rim of the drum. Of the drum. And then you had a little arm come out from the beater. That's right. That's right. And you just hit it there. Well, did it have a padded... No, no. Just like... A piece of metal, actually. Yeah, a piece of metal. Like a ball on the... Yeah. A little round ball. A little round ball. Yeah. A little round ball. I mean, the thing was made in one, but on the end it was round. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, that's the part that hit. Like the ball part that hit. And did you find that that improved the music, the beat, the drumming? Did you find that that was better than the way they have it nowadays without the cymbal? No. No, I think nowadays it's... It's just better. I mean, it is, yeah. They quit using that, so they must like it... Well, man used to play it so loud a long time ago, you know. He used to play loud. Oh, yeah. And then we'd have open cymbal. You see, we had a cymbal called a cry cymbal. And then you wouldn't choke that or nothing. No, they'd create that cymbal. You'd hit it louder than you wanted. Now you see, when we play on Sundays, I mean if we're going to have a dance, Sunday night we'd play the advertising that evening. We'd start on the truck advertising. Well now, that way the drummer and the trombone player had to play loud trumpet too. In other words, you crash cymbal, you had to hit as loud as you can almost, you know, to make everybody never hear you. Yeah, I see. You had to get on the corner. And then bam, bam. So your advertising was always a loud banger. That's right. And bring all the people. Yeah. Your crash cymbal, was that the cymbal with all the little, uh, What, like Coca-Cola top? No, no, it was a larger cymbal but it was very thin. It was a thin, thin. Uh-huh. And it was very loud. Yeah, with thin material. Very, very loud. So you always played loud on the advertising. On the advertising. And before the dance stopped too, they wanted to feel like a big thing. Oh yeah. To get the people in. Yeah, you had to play on the outside by three numbers. And then inside play loud until they start gathering. After that, when you come down normal. Well, uh, these dances, when it got later in the evening, would you, you'd be, uh, you'd be playing real soft or, late in the evening the soft you play or? No, they'd keep that up. Just the same, uh, hard metal. That's just, the ordinary. Just like my wife saying, it's such a different. Yeah, cause the hogs is right in the neighborhood and you'd play loud and, well, say, uh, around, say, twelve o'clock, we'd soften up a little. But after a while, the music would get lively and it just, it just, . And it was nothing said. That police detail, that's all they had to have, just have a police detail at the door and that was it. But nowadays you have to have a permit for all that. Oh yeah, you have to have a permit. Uh huh. And if you don't. Well, you had a permit too, but it wasn't, it didn't cost as much as what it costs. And now, and then you have a limitation of everything now. Before there was no limit. Uh, you mean, uh. You see, you could sort of dance, dance, I say from eight, when they say eight until late, you play until they break the next morning. Wow, yeah. But now you say with the limitation, you have to stop at a certain time. Yeah, yeah. What does it usually cost? Now if you don't get an appointment, you see if you get an appointment. . . .

Okay, you're talking about that permit, how long it runs and all? Yes. Well, the permit now, it just runs until midnight. But if you get it dated for the next day, say like, well then you can have your supper to run that night before and all the next day. Oh, I see. Uh-huh. In other words, you get it dated for two days. Right. But then I suppose that would cost twice as much.
